name: Aurora
title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Aurora, IL | Genstone
metaDescription: Aurora, IL renovation contractor for investors: Fox River historic homes, two-flats and far east side colonials, permits handled, draws tied to finished work.
intro:
Aurora is really several housing markets sharing one city name. On either bank of the Fox River, the older neighborhoods hold Victorian houses, foursquares, workers' homes and two-flats that date back to the city's railroad and manufacturing years. Out on the far east side, along the DuPage County line, the housing is mostly 1980s through 2000s subdivisions that feel closer to Naperville than to downtown. A renovation plan that works in one area can be completely wrong for the other.

Genstone Construction is based just southeast of Aurora in Romeoville, and we coordinate vetted, licensed contractors across the city and the Fox Valley. Each project has a designated field manager, an itemized scope with a draw schedule, and documentation you can review from anywhere.

The free Pre-Offer Rehab Review is the place to start. Before you commit capital, our estimators assess repair costs, refine your ARV against comps on that side of the river, and give you a straight answer on whether the deal works at your price.
housingStock:
Aurora's housing history follows the Fox River and the railroad. The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy shops and dozens of factories drew workers through the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and the neighborhoods around downtown filled with housing for them.

On the near east and near west sides you find Italianate and Queen Anne houses, foursquares, gable-front frame homes and simple workers' cottages, many built between the 1870s and 1920s. Two-flats, front-and-rear duplexes and large houses converted into several apartments are mixed throughout. Historic districts such as Tanner and Riddle Highlands, and the hilltop streets of Pigeon Hill, contain some of the best-preserved examples. These buildings typically have stone or brick foundations, balloon framing, plaster walls, old wiring and galvanized or cast-iron plumbing.

After World War II, ranches, Cape Cods and split-levels filled in the outer edges of the east and west sides. These have poured or block foundations and simpler systems but often include asbestos-containing tiles or siding and original electrical panels that buyers question.

From the 1980s onward, development pushed east toward the Fox Valley mall and the DuPage County line, producing large subdivisions of two-story colonials and townhomes, many served by the Indian Prairie school district. Newer neighborhoods such as Stonebridge and Oakhurst fit this pattern.

For investors, that range means very different rehab exposures. Older river neighborhoods carry the highest mechanical and structural risk but the lowest entry prices. The far east side offers predictable construction and stronger resale but less room for value-add. Most good Aurora deals begin with understanding which of those two you are buying.

There is also a practical middle category worth knowing: early twentieth century bungalows and modest frame houses on the outer blocks of the near west side, built after the boom years but before the war. They tend to have full basements, smaller footprints and fewer additions than the Victorians, and they renovate more cleanly. Investors who want older-home pricing with fewer surprises often focus there first.

commonIssues.title: Old foundations near the river
commonIssues.body: Many homes on the near east and near west sides sit on limestone or brick foundations that have settled, lost mortar or let water in for decades. Bowing walls, cracked mortar and damp basements are common, especially on lots that slope toward the Fox River. These conditions are not always deal-breakers, but they need to be priced accurately. We evaluate foundation condition carefully during the pre-offer review and bring in structural input when walls show movement or water management looks inadequate.

commonIssues.title: Informal conversions
commonIssues.body: Large older houses in Aurora were often divided into multiple apartments over the years, sometimes without permits. That can mean shared electrical services, poor fire separation between units, steep or unsafe rear stairs and basement units without adequate egress. Buyers and lenders may ask about the legal unit count, and the city may as well. We look for signs of unpermitted conversion and help you decide whether to legalize, reduce units or return the house to single-family use.

commonIssues.title: Knob-and-tube and early wiring
commonIssues.body: Homes built before the 1940s in Aurora's older neighborhoods frequently retain sections of knob-and-tube wiring, sometimes extended with later cloth-insulated or ungrounded circuits. Insurers and buyers' inspectors both flag it. Postwar houses may have undersized services or outdated panels. A full or partial rewire is often unavoidable in an older Aurora home, and it is easiest when walls are already open during a renovation. We price electrical work carefully because it frequently becomes one of the largest line items.

commonIssues.title: Lead paint on older exteriors
commonIssues.body: Most houses in the historic river neighborhoods have multiple layers of lead-based paint on siding, porches, windows and trim. Any renovation that disturbs painted surfaces must follow EPA lead-safe work practices, and exterior paint jobs on these houses require careful containment and cleanup. Window replacement in historic districts can also require review. We plan for lead-safe methods from the start and account for the extra labor in the estimate rather than treating it as a surprise.

commonIssues.title: Aging 1980s and 1990s systems
commonIssues.body: On the far east side, problems are less structural and more about age. Roofs, furnaces, air conditioners and water heaters installed when subdivisions were built are often due for replacement. Hardboard siding, aging windows and worn decks are also common. These are predictable costs, and they are exactly what buyers' inspectors focus on in newer suburban homes. We price them clearly so you can decide what to replace before listing and what to disclose.

investorMarket:
Investor strategy in Aurora tends to divide along the river and the county lines.

The near east and near west sides are where most value-add work happens. Purchase prices are lower, the housing stock is older and there is a large supply of two-flats, duplexes and converted houses. These neighborhoods suit buy-and-hold investors, BRRRR deals and small multifamily owners who can manage older buildings. Fix-and-flip projects also work here, particularly with well-built foursquares and bungalows that can be updated without losing their character.

Historic districts such as Tanner and Riddle Highlands attract buyers who value period details. Renovations there should preserve woodwork, stairs and other original features, and exterior changes may need review from the city's preservation commission.

Postwar neighborhoods on the outer east and west sides are a middle ground. Ranches and split-levels are straightforward to renovate and appeal to first-time buyers and renters.

The far east side, especially around Fox Valley and the DuPage County portion, behaves more like Naperville. Homes there are newer, values are higher and buyers expect move-in-ready condition. Flips work when a house is clearly dated compared to neighbors, and rentals appeal to families who want the school district.

Across all areas, property taxes vary by county and taxing district, and Aurora spans four counties, so model taxes for the specific parcel rather than using a citywide estimate.
permits:
Building permits in Aurora are issued by the City of Aurora's building and permits division. Work that typically requires a permit includes roofing, siding, window replacement when openings change, structural repairs, decks, basement finishing, kitchen and bath remodels that alter plumbing or electrical, mechanical replacements and any change in the number of units. Larger projects require plan review before issue, and inspections are scheduled at the rough and final stages.

Aurora has designated historic districts and individual landmarks, and exterior changes in those areas, such as siding, windows, porches and roofing materials, can require review by the city's Historic Preservation Commission before work starts. Planning for that review is important on projects near downtown.

The city also runs property standards enforcement and has rental registration and inspection requirements for residential rentals, which landlords should confirm with the city before leasing. Vacant properties are subject to maintenance standards as well.

Because Aurora spans Kane, DuPage, Will and Kendall counties, some details such as floodplain mapping vary by location. Genstone reviews permit, historic and floodplain questions during scoping so you know the path before work begins.
climate:
Aurora's climate is typical of the western Chicago suburbs, with cold winters, hot and humid summers, and frequent freeze-thaw cycles in late fall and early spring. Those cycles are hard on old stone foundations, front steps and concrete driveways, and on the wood porches common in the river neighborhoods.

The Fox River adds another factor. Heavy spring rain or rapid snowmelt can raise the river and the water table, and low-lying properties near its banks may see basement seepage or flooding. Foundation repair, waterproofing and grading are best handled before interior finishes and ideally before the wettest part of spring.

Exterior work such as painting, masonry, roofing and concrete is most reliable from late spring through early fall. Lead-safe exterior paint jobs especially benefit from dry, mild weather. In winter, we concentrate on interior trades and keep vacant properties heated or properly winterized to prevent frozen pipes in older homes with poorly insulated walls.

faqs.q: Which parts of Aurora do you work in?
faqs.a: We work throughout the city, including the near east and near west sides, the historic districts around downtown, the postwar neighborhoods on the outer east and west sides, and the far east side subdivisions near Fox Valley and the DuPage County line. We also cover neighboring towns such as North Aurora, Montgomery, Oswego and Batavia. Work is performed by vetted, licensed local contractors and managed by a designated Genstone field manager on each project.

faqs.q: Do you renovate homes in Aurora's historic districts?
faqs.a: Yes. Older homes in districts such as Tanner and Riddle Highlands often need careful work that respects original features. Exterior changes in these districts may require review by the city's Historic Preservation Commission. We plan for that review during scoping, specify appropriate materials and use lead-safe practices when disturbing older painted surfaces, which helps keep the project on schedule and avoids having to redo work after the fact.

faqs.q: Are two-flats and converted houses common in Aurora?
faqs.a: They are, especially on the near east and near west sides. Many large older houses were divided into apartments over the decades, and some purpose-built two-flats and duplexes remain. Before buying, confirm the legal unit count with the city. During our pre-offer review we look for signs of unpermitted conversion, such as shared services or poor egress, and price what it would take to bring the building into compliance.

faqs.q: How does Genstone handle payment?
faqs.a: There is no upfront payment. Our construction draws are tied to completed work that is documented with photos and progress notes, and final payment is due only after the project is complete and you have approved it. Estimates include dumpster and debris removal, and lien waivers come from each contractor as they are paid, so you have a clean record when it comes time to sell or refinance.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Aurora, IL | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Aurora fix and flip renovations for river-neighborhood foursquares, postwar ranches and far east side colonials, priced to the right comps and paid in draws.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Aurora
fix-flip.intro:
Flipping in Aurora starts with deciding which Aurora you are selling into. A renovated foursquare on the near west side competes with other older homes at an approachable price point and attracts first-time buyers who want character. A refreshed colonial on the far east side competes with Naperville listings and buyers who expect everything to be done. The scope, finishes and budget for those two flips have almost nothing in common.

Genstone helps Aurora flippers match the rehab to the right buyer. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review looks at the mechanical, foundation and lead-paint exposure in older homes, or the roof and system age in newer ones, and lays out a finish plan tied to the comps that buyers will actually compare your house against.

sections.h2: Flipping older homes on the near east and west sides
sections.body:
The older neighborhoods around downtown Aurora have plenty of houses with good bones, including foursquares, bungalows and gable-front homes with original woodwork and front porches. Buyers here often appreciate those details, so the best flips keep what is worth keeping and modernize what buyers expect: kitchen, baths, electrical, heating and cooling.

The hidden risks are what separate a profitable flip from a painful one. Stone foundations can need tuckpointing or partial rebuilding. Knob-and-tube wiring is common and has to be replaced. Galvanized supply lines restrict water pressure and corrode from the inside. Cast-iron drains may be cracked under the basement floor. And nearly every surface was painted with lead paint at some point.

We identify these issues during the pre-offer review and price them before you commit. That way the flip budget reflects the house you are actually buying, not the version that looked fine in the listing photos. It also helps you decide which houses to pass on.

sections.h2: Flipping far east side Aurora homes
sections.body:
East of Route 59 and around the Fox Valley area, Aurora's housing stock is mostly 1980s through 2000s colonials, ranches and townhomes. Many sit in the Indian Prairie school district, which draws buyers who might otherwise look only in Naperville. Expectations are high: an updated kitchen with quartz or granite, refreshed baths, new flooring, modern lighting and fresh paint throughout.

The opportunity in this part of Aurora is usually the house that never got updated. Original oak cabinets, builder-grade fixtures, worn carpet, an aging roof and a furnace from the year the house was built all reduce value compared to renovated neighbors. Fixing them is predictable work, and the price gap between dated and updated houses can support a solid flip margin.

Buyers' inspectors in this area focus on roofs, mechanical age, windows and siding. We price those items alongside the cosmetic work so the house holds up at inspection. In HOA neighborhoods, we check exterior rules before choosing materials or colors.

sections.h2: Scheduling an Aurora flip around permits and seasons
sections.body:
Aurora flips are often won or lost on timing. In older neighborhoods, permits for electrical, plumbing and structural work take longer to prepare than cosmetic updates, and work in historic districts may require additional review before exterior changes. We start that paperwork immediately after closing, or before if your contract allows, so the trades are not waiting on approvals.

Seasonality matters too. Buyer activity in Aurora, like the rest of the western suburbs, picks up in spring and stays strong into summer. Exterior work, including painting, roofing, porches and concrete, is best done in warmer months, especially lead-safe painting on older homes. If you buy in winter, we focus on interior trades first and line up exterior work for the first good weather window so the house can list when buyers return.

Throughout the project, your field manager provides photos and progress notes tied to each draw. That keeps you and your lender informed without visits, and it gives you documentation to share with buyers about what was replaced.

faqs.q: Which Aurora homes make the best flips?
faqs.a: Older homes near downtown with solid structure and original character often make strong flips when the systems can be updated within budget. Postwar ranches and split-levels are dependable middle-market flips. On the far east side, dated colonials in good school districts can support a profitable renovation if the purchase price reflects their condition. Our pre-offer review compares your target against local comps and gives you a realistic repair estimate so you can judge the margin.

faqs.q: Do I need to worry about historic district rules on a flip?
faqs.a: If the property is in a designated historic district or is an individual landmark, exterior changes such as siding, windows, porches and roofing materials may need review by Aurora's Historic Preservation Commission. Interior work typically does not. We check the property's status during scoping and plan the exterior scope accordingly, which helps avoid delays or having to redo work that did not meet district guidelines.

faqs.q: How do you handle lead paint on older Aurora flips?
faqs.a: Any work that disturbs painted surfaces in a pre-1978 home must follow EPA lead-safe practices, which involve containment, specialized cleanup and trained workers. In Aurora's older neighborhoods that applies to most flips. We include the additional labor and materials in our estimate, so lead-safe work is budgeted from the start rather than added as a change order midway through the project.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Aurora, IL | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: Aurora BRRRR renovations for older single-family homes and two-flats, scoped to appraise on refinance and hold up to tenants, with draws tied to completed work.
brrrr.intro:
Aurora is one of the more practical BRRRR markets in the western suburbs. The older neighborhoods on both sides of the Fox River offer houses and small multifamily buildings at prices well below the far east side, and rental demand is steady from families, commuters and workers tied to the area's warehouses, hospitals and manufacturers. The challenge is renovating an older building so it appraises well and holds up for years without overspending.

Genstone builds Aurora BRRRR scopes around both goals. We focus on the systems and finishes that appraisers recognize and tenants do not easily damage. Through Genstone Financial you can also look at fix-and-flip loans for acquisition and rehab and DSCR rental loans for the refinance, coordinated with the renovation schedule.

sections.h2: Where Aurora BRRRR deals tend to work
sections.body:
The best BRRRR opportunities in Aurora usually come from the near east and near west sides, where older single-family homes and two-flats sell at lower prices and need enough work to create a value gap. Postwar ranches and Cape Cods on the outer parts of the city are another option, with less structural risk and simpler systems.

The key is a reliable appraisal after renovation. In older neighborhoods, appraisers compare your property against other renovated homes and two-flats nearby, so the rehab needs to bring it up to that standard. Houses that are significantly larger, smaller or more unusual than surrounding properties can be harder to appraise, which is worth considering before purchase.

Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates the cost of bringing a specific Aurora property to a rentable, appraisable condition and compares it against recent sales. We are not appraisers, but that comparison helps you judge whether the refinance is likely to return enough capital to keep the strategy going.

sections.h2: Renovating older Aurora homes to appraise
sections.body:
Appraisers value permanent, visible improvements and functional systems. In an older Aurora home, that typically means a new or updated kitchen, renovated bathrooms, refinished hardwood or new durable flooring, replacement windows, a sound roof, and updated electrical, plumbing and heating. A house with knob-and-tube wiring or a failing foundation will struggle to appraise well, even with attractive finishes.

We prioritize these items in the scope. Rewiring older homes, replacing galvanized supply lines and old cast-iron drains, addressing foundation and water issues, and installing efficient heating and cooling all support value and reduce future repairs. Finishes are chosen to look clean and current without premium pricing.

At the end of the project, we compile documentation of completed permits, new equipment and before and after photos. Giving that package to the appraiser helps them see the full scope of the work, especially in older houses where improvements to wiring and plumbing are hidden in the walls and not obvious during a short visit.

Rental durability in Aurora's older housing means choosing materials that stand up to daily use, cleaning and turnover while respecting the character buyers and appraisers value. We often refinish original hardwood in living areas, install luxury vinyl plank in kitchens, baths and basements, and use durable paint with semi-gloss on trim and doors.

Kitchens get solid cabinets, quartz or laminate counters and appliances with readily available service parts. Bathrooms get tile or solid-surface surrounds, good ventilation fans to prevent moisture damage, and standard fixtures. Exterior items such as gutters, downspouts and grading are corrected to keep water away from old foundations.

In two-flats and duplexes, separate utilities can significantly improve net income. Adding separate electrical services, heating systems and water heaters for each unit allows tenants to pay their own costs, which improves cash flow and the property's performance under a DSCR loan. We include those upgrades where they make sense and coordinate permits and utility work with the city and providers.

faqs.q: Is Aurora a good market for BRRRR?
faqs.a: It can be, particularly in the older neighborhoods near downtown and in postwar areas where purchase prices leave room for value-add renovation. Steady rental demand from local employers and commuters supports long-term holds. The deal still depends on buying well and renovating efficiently. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review helps you test whether a specific property can support your refinance goal before you commit capital to it.

faqs.q: Do you handle permits for BRRRR projects in Aurora?
faqs.a: Yes. Electrical, plumbing, structural, mechanical and roofing work all typically require permits from the City of Aurora. We prepare and submit them, schedule inspections and keep records of every sign-off. Those records are helpful at refinance, since they show the appraiser and lender that the improvements were completed properly and inspected by the city. In older river-area homes, where much of the value sits inside the walls, that paper trail carries real weight.

faqs.q: Can I finance my Aurora BRRRR with Genstone Financial?
faqs.a: Genstone Financial, part of the Genstone Companies, offers fix-and-flip loans for acquisition and renovation, DSCR rental loans for the refinance, lines of credit and new construction loans. Approval depends on their underwriting. You can also use any other lender, and we will provide the scope, estimate, draw schedule and documentation they require to release funds. Lining up the draw schedule with the lender early prevents gaps that leave trades waiting.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Aurora, IL | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Single-family rental renovation in Aurora, IL: older river-neighborhood homes and newer east side houses made tenant-ready, durable and inspection-ready.
rental-renovation.intro:
Aurora rental owners deal with two very different kinds of property. Older homes near the Fox River tend to have high maintenance needs, from aging foundations to outdated wiring, while newer homes on the far east side mostly need system replacements and cosmetic refreshes. A rental renovation plan in Aurora should reflect which type of house you own and what is likely to fail next.

Genstone renovates single-family rentals in Aurora for individual landlords, funds and institutional owners. We focus on systems that generate service calls, finishes that can be cleaned and repaired quickly, and documentation that makes the next turnover simpler. Genstone Field Services can also provide inspections, occupied maintenance and turns after the renovation is complete.

sections.h2: Reducing maintenance in older Aurora rentals
sections.body:
In the river neighborhoods, most rental headaches trace back to age. Basement water from old stone or brick foundations, frozen pipes in uninsulated exterior walls, failing boilers or furnaces, overloaded circuits on old wiring and clogged cast-iron drains top the list.

A rental renovation should tackle these problems while the house is empty. We repoint or repair foundation walls where needed, correct grading and extend downspouts to reduce basement water, insulate or reroute vulnerable supply lines, and replace aging heating equipment. Where wiring is outdated, we upgrade the service and replace old circuits, especially in kitchens and baths. A sewer camera inspection can catch root intrusion or broken pipes before they cause a backup.

These steps cost more than a basic make-ready, but they can significantly reduce emergency calls and keep tenants longer. They also help when an Aurora rental is inspected under the city's rental requirements, because many common violations relate to these same systems and safety items.

sections.h2: Refreshing newer east side rental homes
sections.body:
Rental homes on Aurora's far east side, especially those in sought-after school districts, attract tenants with higher expectations. These homes are newer, but many have aging roofs, original windows, worn carpet and furnaces or air conditioners nearing the end of their lives.

Our renovations here focus on durability and appeal. We replace worn carpet with luxury vinyl plank in main living areas, update kitchen counters and fixtures, refresh bathrooms, paint throughout and replace mechanical equipment that is near the end of its service life. Exterior work may include new roofs, repaired siding and new gutters. If the home is in an HOA, we confirm material and color rules before ordering.

These homes command higher rents, but tenants also compare them to similar homes for sale or rent in neighboring Naperville and Oswego. Keeping the property in strong condition helps reduce vacancy and supports better long-term returns. We document every upgrade so future maintenance and turn work starts from a clear record of equipment ages and finish selections.

sections.h2: Standards, turns and documentation for Aurora portfolios
sections.body:
Owners with multiple Aurora rentals benefit from a consistent renovation standard. Using the same flooring, paint, fixtures and appliances across properties makes repairs faster and helps vendors keep parts on hand. Genstone can help you define a standard suited to both older and newer Aurora homes, or apply one you already use.

Turnovers are the best time to keep homes competitive. Our turn scopes typically include paint, flooring repair or replacement, fixture updates, appliance checks and exterior maintenance. We also verify smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, stair railings and bedroom window operation, since these are common inspection items.

Every renovation and turn ends with photo documentation and a summary of completed work. That record helps when evaluating security deposits, responding to a city rental inspection or planning future capital expenses. It also makes it easier to compare performance across your Aurora properties over time and decide where the next round of upgrades will pay off.

faqs.q: Does Aurora require rental inspections?
faqs.a: Aurora has rental registration and inspection requirements administered by the city, and landlords should confirm current rules with the city before leasing. During our renovation we address common inspection items such as smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, handrails, egress, electrical safety and heating, which helps prepare the property, though passing any inspection depends on the city's own review of the home.

faqs.q: Can you renovate rentals across both sides of Aurora?
faqs.a: Yes. We work in the older neighborhoods near downtown and the newer subdivisions on the far east side, as well as surrounding towns. Older homes usually need system upgrades and structural attention, while newer ones mainly need equipment replacement and cosmetic refreshes. We tailor the scope to the property type so your budget goes where it does the most good.

faqs.q: What warranty comes with an Aurora rental renovation?
faqs.a: Genstone provides a one-year workmanship warranty on our work. It covers defects in workmanship but not tenant damage or normal wear and tear. To help with that distinction, we provide photo documentation at the end of every renovation, which makes it easier to evaluate the condition of the home at move-out and handle security deposit decisions fairly. Any workmanship issue within the year goes back to your field manager.

multifamily-renovation.title: Two-Flat & 2–4 Unit Renovation in Aurora, IL | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Aurora two-flat, duplex and converted-house renovations: shared systems, unit legality, occupied phasing and historic-district exterior work near downtown.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Two-Flat and Small Multifamily Renovation in Aurora
multifamily-renovation.intro:
Aurora has one of the deepest supplies of small multifamily housing in the western suburbs. Near downtown, on both sides of the Fox River, you find purpose-built two-flats, front-and-rear duplexes, and large Victorian and foursquare houses split into three or four apartments over the past century. For investors, these buildings offer more rentable units per dollar than almost anything else in the Fox Valley.

They also come with shared systems, mixed construction histories and questions about legal unit count. Genstone renovates Aurora's 2–4 unit buildings as whole structures, starting with foundations, roofs, utilities and egress, then moving into individual units. We phase work around occupied apartments and confirm the building's legal status questions before you plan on rent from every unit.

sections.h2: Converted houses and legal unit count
sections.body:
Many small multifamily properties in Aurora began life as large single-family houses. Over the decades they were divided into apartments, sometimes with city approval and sometimes without. That history affects both value and renovation scope.

Signs of an informal conversion include a single electrical service feeding multiple units, shared heating with no separate controls, units accessed only through another unit, rear stairs that do not meet current standards and basement apartments without proper egress windows. Fire separation between units may be missing or inadequate.

Before purchasing, confirm the legal number of units with the City of Aurora. During the pre-offer review, Genstone looks for physical clues and prices what it would take to bring the building into compliance or to reduce the unit count. That comparison helps you understand the true cost of the property. Sometimes legalizing every unit makes sense. Other times, a well-renovated two-unit building is a better investment than a crowded three-unit one that cannot pass inspection.

sections.h2: Shared systems in older Aurora buildings
sections.body:
In two-flats and converted houses near downtown Aurora, the foundation, roof, sewer line and often the heating system serve every unit. Problems with any of them affect all tenants and can make or break the renovation budget.

Foundation issues are common in older stone and brick foundations, especially on sloped lots near the river. Roofs may have multiple layers or failing flashing at dormers and porches. Sewer lines are often clay or cast iron and may be damaged by roots. Shared boilers or furnaces can be old and inefficient.

We evaluate these elements first, then decide with you whether to separate systems or keep them shared. Separating heating and electrical services allows tenants to pay their own utilities and improves net income, but it requires permits and coordination with utility providers. In some buildings, a new shared high-efficiency system with heat included in rent makes more sense. We price both options so the choice is based on numbers, not guesswork.

Many Aurora two-flats and converted houses come with tenants in place. Renovating around them requires careful planning, both for safety and to keep rental income flowing during the project.

We typically start with work in vacant units and on building systems that must be addressed first. Water, gas and electrical interruptions are scheduled in advance and kept as short as possible. In older buildings, lead-safe practices are essential when disturbing painted surfaces, and dust containment protects occupied units and shared stairs.

Exterior work, including porches, roofing and siding, is usually done in one phase to keep materials consistent and reduce disruption. If the building is in a historic district, exterior changes may need approval from the city's preservation commission before work begins.

Our field manager coordinates with you on tenant notices and keeps hallways, stairs and exits clear. Each phase is documented with photos and progress notes tied to draws, so you can monitor the work without being on site.

faqs.q: Can I buy a converted house in Aurora and rent every unit?
faqs.a: Only if the units are legal. Many Aurora conversions were done decades ago, and not all were permitted. Confirm the legal unit count with the city before purchase. Our pre-offer review looks for signs of unpermitted conversion and estimates the cost to legalize or reduce units, so you can make an informed decision about the building before your contingency period ends.

faqs.q: Should I separate utilities in my Aurora two-flat?
faqs.a: In many cases it improves net income by letting tenants pay their own heat and electricity, which also helps under DSCR loan underwriting. It requires permits, licensed trades and coordination with utility companies. In some buildings, especially with older boiler systems, a new shared system may be more practical. We price both approaches so you can compare them side by side.

faqs.q: How do you handle lead paint in older Aurora buildings?
faqs.a: Most of Aurora's small multifamily buildings near downtown were built well before 1978 and contain lead paint. We follow EPA lead-safe practices on any work that disturbs painted surfaces, including containment, specialized cleanup and trained workers. That protects occupied units and helps you comply with federal rules for rental housing when tenants are present. Window replacement often removes the biggest lead hazards at friction surfaces.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Aurora, IL | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor in Aurora, IL: older foursquares, two-flats and east side homes, Standard and Limited bids, consultant coordination and draws.
fha-203k.intro:
Aurora is a natural fit for FHA 203(k) financing. The city has a large supply of older homes and two-flats near downtown that need updates buyers cannot easily fund on top of a down payment, and many first-time buyers are drawn to Aurora because it offers more space and character for the money than neighboring suburbs. A 203(k) loan lets them buy and renovate with one mortgage.

As an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor headquartered one town over in Romeoville, Genstone Construction knows this program well. We work with Aurora buyers, agents and lenders to prepare program-ready bids, coordinate with HUD consultants on Standard loans, handle permits with the City of Aurora and complete the work through inspected draws, with no upfront payment from the borrower.

sections.h2: Matching Aurora homes to Standard or Limited 203(k)
sections.body:
The type of 203(k) loan depends on the work the house needs, and Aurora's mix of housing makes that decision especially important.

The Limited 203(k) covers non-structural repairs up to $75,000. It suits postwar ranches and Cape Cods, and newer homes on the far east side that need kitchens, baths, flooring, roofs, windows, furnaces or water heaters. Many solid homes in Aurora fall into this category.

The Standard 203(k) is needed for structural work or larger projects. Older foursquares and Victorians near downtown often require foundation repair, porch rebuilding, rewiring and full plumbing replacement, which can push the work into Standard territory. It carries a $5,000 minimum repair amount and requires a HUD-approved 203(k) consultant.

Owner-occupants can also use 203(k) loans on two to four unit properties, which makes Aurora's two-flats and duplexes attractive to buyers who want rental income from the other units. We help agents and buyers determine the right loan type early in the process.

sections.h2: Preparing a 203(k) bid for an older Aurora house
sections.body:
Older Aurora homes can hide problems that surface once walls are opened. A good 203(k) bid anticipates as many of them as possible, so the loan amount reflects reality.

Genstone's estimators prepare itemized bids that list each trade, specify materials and include permit fees and debris removal. In older homes, we look closely at foundation condition, wiring, plumbing, heating, roof layers and lead paint. Where the HUD consultant prepares a work write-up on a Standard loan, our bid follows its structure so the lender can match the two.

We also discuss priorities with the buyer and agent. Some items, such as a failing foundation or knob-and-tube wiring, must be addressed. Others, such as kitchen finishes, can be scaled to fit the loan. If the house is in a historic district, exterior changes may need review by the city's preservation commission, which we account for in the bid and schedule. We provide our licensing and insurance documentation with the bid.

sections.h2: Draws, permits and changes during the project
sections.body:
After closing, renovation funds are placed in escrow and released in draws as work is completed and inspected. Genstone does not require upfront payment, and our draw schedule follows the program's requirements.

We obtain permits from the City of Aurora and schedule inspections. On Standard loans, the HUD consultant inspects completed work before each draw. On Limited loans, the lender verifies progress according to its process. Our field manager keeps the buyer, agent and lender updated with photos and notes.

In older Aurora homes, unexpected conditions are common. If we find rotted framing behind plaster, damaged drain lines under the basement floor or additional wiring issues, we document them and provide pricing so the consultant and lender can approve use of the contingency reserve. Clear documentation keeps the project moving and avoids disputes. Lien waivers are provided with each payment, and the buyer receives a complete record of the work at the end of the project.

faqs.q: Can I use an FHA 203(k) loan on an Aurora two-flat?
faqs.a: Yes, as long as you live in one of the units as your primary residence. The program covers one to four unit properties, which makes it useful for buying and renovating Aurora's two-flats and duplexes. Rental income from the other unit may help with qualifying, depending on your lender's guidelines. We prepare bids that cover the whole building, including shared systems and each unit.

faqs.q: What kinds of Aurora homes need a Standard 203(k)?
faqs.a: Homes that need structural work, such as foundation repair, porch rebuilding or removing load-bearing walls, or total repairs above $75,000, require the Standard program. Older homes near downtown often fall into this category because of their age and condition. Newer or postwar homes needing cosmetic and system updates usually fit the Limited program instead. Your lender makes the final call, and we write the bid to support it.

faqs.q: How quickly can you provide a 203(k) bid in Aurora?
faqs.a: We work to fit the timeline of your purchase contract and lender, and we know 203(k) deals often run under tight deadlines. Our estimators can usually visit the property promptly after an accepted offer and prepare an itemized bid. Contact us as early as possible, ideally before your inspection period begins, so there is time to coordinate with the consultant and lender.

reo-renovation.title: REO & Bank-Owned Renovation in Aurora, IL | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: REO renovation in Aurora for servicers, banks and GSEs: older vacant homes, freeze and water damage, code and rental compliance, documented scopes and draws.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovation in Aurora
reo-renovation.intro:
Bank-owned property in Aurora spans everything from century-old houses and two-flats near the Fox River to newer suburban homes on the far east side. The older stock tends to come with the heaviest repair needs: aging systems, foundation issues, lead paint and the damage that accumulates while a house sits empty. Newer REO homes usually need cleanup, system repairs and cosmetic refreshes.

Our REO clients range from banks and mortgage servicers to REITs, investment funds and Government-Sponsored Enterprises, which have named Genstone a preferred contractor. In Aurora, we coordinate licensed local contractors, manage permits with the city and provide documentation and reporting aligned with asset management requirements, from initial inspection through final billing.

sections.h2: Common conditions in vacant Aurora REO
sections.body:
Vacant older homes in Aurora deteriorate in predictable ways. Winter freeze damage is a major risk when properties are not properly winterized, causing burst pipes, damaged radiators or baseboard heat, and water-soaked plaster ceilings. Old foundations may let in water during spring thaw or heavy rain, leading to mold in basements and on framing.

Vandalism and theft can occur in long-vacant properties, including removal of copper piping and appliances. Exterior neglect, such as overgrown yards, damaged porches and broken windows, can attract code violations.

Newer far east side REO homes are more likely to have basement water damage from failed sump pumps, mold from roof or plumbing leaks, and HOA violations for exterior maintenance.

Genstone documents all conditions during the initial inspection and separates urgent stabilization, such as removing water, securing openings and addressing safety hazards, from the full renovation scope. This allows asset managers to approve emergency work immediately while deciding on the broader plan for each property.

sections.h2: Code compliance and property standards in Aurora
sections.body:
The City of Aurora enforces property maintenance standards on vacant homes, covering items such as securing doors and windows, removing debris and maintaining yards. Older properties may also have open permits or code violations that need to be resolved before resale.

Genstone reviews visible violations and open permits during scoping and includes required corrections in the renovation plan. Where properties are in historic districts, exterior repairs may need review by the city's preservation commission, which we account for in the schedule.

Genstone Field Services offers property preservation, inspections, occupied maintenance and code compliance services. That can keep a vacant Aurora REO secure and compliant while the asset manager evaluates options. When renovation begins, we handle permits and inspections, and our records document every step. Buyers' attorneys and lenders often ask about open permits and violations, so resolving them early helps keep closings on schedule and reduces surprises late in the sale.

sections.h2: Renovation scopes matched to Aurora disposition plans
sections.body:
The right REO renovation scope depends on how the property will be sold or held. Many older Aurora REO homes will be sold to owner-occupants using conventional or FHA financing. Those buyers and lenders need working mechanical systems, a sound roof, safe stairs and porches, functional kitchens and baths, and no peeling lead paint.

Some REO assets are better suited for investors or rental portfolios. For those, the scope may focus on durable finishes, separate utilities in two-flats and fixes that reduce ongoing maintenance.

Genstone provides scopes and estimates with labor, materials and draw schedules, often with multiple options when the disposition plan is still being decided. When an Aurora REO is likely to sell to a buyer using 203(k) renovation financing, our certification under that program lets us bid the post-sale work as well. Each project concludes with inspection sign-offs, photo documentation and lien waivers from all contractors, giving asset managers a complete record for reporting and resale. On older Aurora properties near the river, we also include foundation and drainage notes so the disposition team understands any lingering water risk.

faqs.q: Do you work with servicers and GSEs on Aurora properties?
faqs.a: Yes. Servicers, banks, REITs, funds and GSEs are a core part of our client base, and Genstone holds preferred contractor status with Government-Sponsored Enterprises. We provide detailed scopes, estimates, photo documentation and lien waivers in formats suited to asset management reporting, with a designated manager assigned to each Aurora property so communication stays consistent from start to finish. Bid formats can match your platform.

faqs.q: Can you secure and maintain an Aurora REO before renovation?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone Field Services provides property preservation, including securing openings, debris removal, lawn care, winterization and periodic inspections. These services help keep a vacant property compliant with city standards and prevent further deterioration while the asset manager decides on renovation or sale. Inspection reports and photos are provided after each visit. That history also helps us scope the renovation faster once it is approved.

faqs.q: What happens if an Aurora REO has unpermitted work?
faqs.a: We identify signs of unpermitted work during our inspection, such as unapproved unit conversions, additions or electrical changes. The asset manager can then decide whether to legalize the work, remove it or sell the property as-is. If correction is chosen, we prepare a scope, obtain permits from the City of Aurora and complete the work with required inspections. Closed permits then go into the property file.
